rule: A ✓ means a published, machine-checked proof shows that all the code computing the operation, as that library runs it on that host, gives the specified result for every input: the cipher and its mode, the hash over every block with its padding, the whole scalar multiplication or exponentiation, and the glue around them, such as clamping, byte conversion, and point encoding. Parsing DER key and signature containers, randomness, and the message hash a signature takes are left out. Proofs of memory safety alone, or of only some of the code, earn no ✓.

Not ranked: a JWT's `load` rows: aws-lc-rs's provider parses the key only when it signs or verifies, so only `token`, which includes loading, compares

gaps.reason: Without SSE4.1 rind runs Graviola's scalar Poly1305 rather than port BoringSSL's SSE2 `poly1305_vec.c` for CPUs older than Westmere, as ALGORITHMS.md records.

AES header protection on aarch64 reaches the key's cipher through an indirect call, as ALGORITHMS.md notes, which costs 3.75 ns against aws-lc-rs's 2.89 ns for one AES-128 block, and 3.72 against 3.13 for AES-256.

The portable backend runs aws-lc's `aes_nohw.c` in its 64-bit configuration, four blocks a pass ([#621](https://github.com/kixel-ai/rind/pull/621)), while this row builds aws-lc's C for x86_64, where it bitslices eight blocks into SSE2 registers: the configuration aws-lc itself runs on the other 64-bit targets the backend is for is rind's. In [run 44941104585](https://github.com/kixel-ai/rind/actions/runs/44941104585) AES-256-GCM measured 1.10× at 16 KB, AES-CTR 1.18 to 1.35× from 1200 B, and CBC decryption 1.22 to 1.30×; shorter messages and the other AES-GCM rows are within 10%.

rind's portable SHA-1 trails aws-lc's C by 1.11 to 1.24× from 1200 B up in [run 44941104585](https://github.com/kixel-ai/rind/actions/runs/44941104585). SHA-1 survives only for legacy signatures and HMAC-SHA-1, which are rare on targets without assembly, so it stays rather than take aws-lc's integer `sha1_block_data_order_nohw`, which armv7 without NEON already runs, as a speed quest.

Unwrapping a 16-byte AES-128 key takes 39 ns more than aws-lc-rs's 323 ns on the EPYC 7763 runner of [run 44941104585](https://github.com/kixel-ai/rind/actions/runs/44941104585), 1.12× its time, as it took 1.11 to 1.20× on the EPYC runners of the run before; the Xeon 6975P native tier unwraps it in 0.95× aws-lc-rs's time, wrapping, every longer key, and the other tiers are within 10%, and aarch64 unwraps in 0.68×. Key wrap is rare and runs once per stored key, so the fixed cost stays without a quest; the next refresh rechecks it.

Decided in [kixel-ai/rind#812](https://github.com/kixel-ai/rind/pull/812): on x86_64 without AVX-512, ML-KEM-768 key generation stays on rind's arithmetic though pyca/verified-garbage's is faster, since a key pair decapsulates on the arithmetic that generated it and VG's decapsulation was 1.17 to 1.25× slower there when it decided, and decapsulation is the hot path. aarch64 holds for the same reason: on `kixtop`'s Apple M4 VG generated keys in 5.22 µs against rind's 6.36 but decapsulated in 4.79 against 4.21 (1.14×), and `ovh-iad` and `ovh-sea` decapsulated at 1.16 and 1.21× rind's time.

quest.title: ristretto255's variable-base multiplication runs curve25519-dalek's AVX2 formulas
AES-GCM on Zen 5 runs verified-garbage's AVX-512 kernels where they are faster

gaps.reason: Not like for like: pyca/verified-garbage's rows import the key on each call from components already parsed, while rind's parse the DER public key on each call, as `UnparsedPublicKey` and rustls do. With [#952](https://github.com/kixel-ai/rind/pull/952), which runs VG's `R² mod n` on key load, `fedora`'s first quiet run since measured 5.45 and 5.83 µs against VG's 4.84 and 5.29 (1.13 and 1.10×; aws-lc-rs 10.0 and 10.6): the difference is that per-call DER parse and re-encoding, the wipe of the key on drop that AGENTS.md requires, and the modulus's conversion to the routine's big-endian bytes. The next refresh rechecks it.

1.11× pyca/verified-garbage's time on `ovh-iad` (66.2 against 59.5 µs), and 1.08× in its other quiet run of the same commit, while `ovh-sea` measured 1.06×, `fedora` 1.06× (16.7 against 15.8 µs), and `nixos` within 10%. rind already runs VG's `d·G` for each signature's `k·G` ([#847](https://github.com/kixel-ai/rind/pull/847)), so the difference is in rind's other steps, among them its hedged nonce: fresh randomness for each signature, as aws-lc-rs draws, where VG derives its nonce deterministically by RFC 6979. That behavior is deliberate, so it stays; the next refresh rechecks the margin.

Noise: other tenants share `ovh-iad`'s VPS, whose load the report cannot see. Its first quiet run of the same commit measured both within 10%, ML-KEM-768 encapsulation at 1.01× pyca/verified-garbage's time (rind runs VG's routine there) and XChaCha20-Poly1305 at 16 KB at 0.98× aws-lc-rs's, as `ovh-sea` did (0.99 and 1.03×); that run's own four gaps, 1.12 to 1.24×, were within 10% in this one. The next refresh rechecks them.
